address_historical: Northwest corner Fifth Avenue and Monroe Street; later 200-208 W Monroe Street
address_modern: Northwest corner Wells Street and West Monroe Street
original_use: wholesale clothing store and loft building
structural_system: load-bearing masonry exterior and party walls; cast-iron interior columns/pilasters; timber girders and wood joists; iron, Lemont stone and pressed-brick facade
postfire_code_context: Post-fire commercial construction emphasized masonry and iron, broad daylight openings, heavy floor capacity and fire-prevention equipment.
notes: The 1879 initial building had five stories plus basement; two stories were added in 1888. HABS identifies cast-iron members continuing from foundation to roof as an important step toward skeletal framing, but the building was not a complete metal skeleton. A contemporary account gives approximately 82 ft 10 in by 102 ft 6 in and an estimated $125,000 cost.

canonical_name: Field, Leiter & Co. State Street store occupancy
alternate_names: Singer Building II; later Marshall Field State Street store phase
address_historical: Northeast corner State and Washington Streets
owner_or_developer: Singer estate; purchased by Field, Leiter & Co.
structural_system: masonry commercial building; exact 1879 fit-out materials not established
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Singer Building destroyed by fire and replaced in 1878
postfire_code_context: The underlying replacement belonged to post-fire masonry commercial rebuilding; this row does not claim new 1879 construction.
notes: Field and Leiter purchased the 1878 replacement building on February 28, 1879, secured surrender of Carson Pirie's lease, fitted it for their business, and received customers there by April. Retained as a property and occupancy phase only.

canonical_name: United States Government Building west-basement post-office phase
alternate_names: Chicago Post Office and Custom House; Mullett Government Building
address_historical: Block bounded by Adams, Clark, Jackson and Dearborn Streets
address_modern: Kluczynski Federal Building and Federal Center site
original_use: post office, custom house and federal offices
architect_or_builder: Alfred B. Mullett; construction administration by federal successors
structural_system: masonry federal building with iron structural and fireproofing systems; phase details require federal specifications
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: 1859 Custom House and Post Office destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire
postfire_code_context: Long-running federal masonry construction embodied post-fire fire-resistance goals; exact assemblies should be verified from federal drawings.
notes: The west half of the basement was finished and turned over for temporary post-office quarters in April 1879. Final building completion was in 1880, so this is not a 1879 whole-building completion despite simplified later references to an 1879 federal building.

address_historical: Southeast corner State and Randolph Streets
original_use: music hall, public assembly, offices and stores
owner_or_developer: Central Music Hall stock company; George B. Carpenter promoter; Levi Z. Leiter president
structural_system: fireproof masonry commercial and assembly building with gray cut-stone exterior
postfire_code_context: The building's fireproof construction, abundant exits, ventilation and public-assembly safeguards responded directly to post-fire and theater-safety concerns.
notes: Erected and opened in 1879. Later descriptions give a 125-by-150-foot footprint, six stories plus basement, two elevators, stores and offices; seating is variously reported around 1,800 to 2,000. The December 1879 inspection emphasizes acoustics, rapid air exchange, multiple exits and fire-safety planning.

address_historical: Southeast corner Randolph Street and Wabash Avenue; 64-66 Wabash Avenue
structural_system: brick-and-steel walls; two freight elevators
postfire_code_context: A tall masonry-and-metal commercial block reflects the post-fire move toward durable loft construction.
notes: A later guide reports erection in 1879, 200 feet on Randolph by 40 feet on Wabash, five stories, 85 feet high and two freight elevators. The architect and the exact sequence of later height changes and demolition remain unresolved.

alternate_names: Cyrus McCormick Mansion; Nettie Fowler McCormick House
address_historical: 135 Rush Street at Erie Street; southeast corner Rush and Huron/Erie block
owner_or_developer: Cyrus H. and Nettie Fowler McCormick
structural_system: Lake Superior sandstone masonry; German Renaissance residence; interior structural system not fully documented
postfire_code_context: The masonry mansion was erected after the 1874 citywide restriction on new wood construction.
notes: The residence was four years in construction, beginning in 1875 and occupied in 1879; a major social dedication followed in May 1880. Contemporary description records three principal stories, brown sandstone, a concert hall and advanced electrical apparatus.

canonical_name: Samuel M. Nickerson House construction start
address_historical: 40 Erie Street
structural_system: fire-resistant masonry residence with extensive stone, tile and metal; detailed assemblies documented by HABS
postfire_code_context: The project was explicitly conceived as a fireproof residence in post-fire Chicago.
notes: Commissioned in 1879 and completed in 1883 at a reported cost of about $450,000. Included for the documented 1879 project start, not counted as a 1879 completion.

alternate_names: James Otis School; James Otis World Language Academy predecessor
address_historical: Armour Street
structural_system: brick masonry; heating recorded as steam by Andreas but coal stoves by CPS history
postfire_code_context: Brick school construction complied with the post-1874 prohibition on new wood buildings; the heating conflict remains unresolved.
notes: Andreas's visually checked school table records erection in 1879, 107 by 88 feet, three stories, 945 sittings and $37,000 total including heating and furniture. CPS says it opened during the 1878-79 academic year and initially used coal stoves and gas; this may indicate a start/opening/completion sequence or a table error.

address_historical: Southwest corner Wood and Congress Streets
address_modern: Cook County medical-campus vicinity near W Harrison St and S Wood St
structural_system: brick masonry; steam heating
postfire_code_context: Brick school construction complied with the post-1874 prohibition on new wood buildings.
notes: Andreas's visually checked 1879 table records 107.5 by 84 feet, three stories, steam heat, 945 sittings and $37,000 including heating and furniture. A later guide independently places the 1879 school at Wood and Congress but gives 800 capacity and $45,000 cost; Andreas controls the annual values pending Board proceedings.

address_historical: Wabash Avenue at Thirty-sixth Place
structural_system: brick masonry; steam heating
postfire_code_context: Brick school construction complied with the post-1874 prohibition on new wood buildings.
notes: Andreas's visually checked table records erection in 1879, 70 by 84 feet, three stories, steam heat, 770 sittings and $29,500 total including heating and furniture. A later addition is reported for 1886; the surviving fabric and exact original footprint require Board and fire-insurance-map review.

canonical_name: Kedzie Avenue bridge over the Illinois and Michigan Canal
address_historical: Kedzie Avenue over the Illinois and Michigan Canal
address_modern: Kedzie Avenue near the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal corridor
owner_or_developer: Town of Cicero with shared public expense
structural_system: single-span wrought-iron bridge
postfire_code_context: Wrought iron provided a durable noncombustible crossing; this site lay in adjacent Cicero rather than within the 1879 city boundary.
notes: Completed March 1, 1879. Retained as metropolitan infrastructure tied to Chicago circulation, but flagged because the contemporary jurisdiction was the Town of Cicero.

address_historical: South end of LaSalle Street tunnel
address_modern: LaSalle Street at the Chicago River
structural_system: material not stated
postfire_code_context: A public-safety access improvement to major post-fire municipal infrastructure; material and ordinance details are not stated.
notes: Andreas reports that a footbridge was placed over the south end of the LaSalle Street tunnel in January 1879. Exact span, material and removal date remain unknown.

address_historical: Lock Street crossing
address_modern: Near present Chicago River and Lock Street alignment
owner_or_developer: Illinois and Michigan Canal Commissioners; State of Illinois
structural_system: wood
postfire_code_context: The wooden construction was an explicit exception or jurisdictional edge case relative to Chicago's 1874 citywide prohibition on new wood buildings; legal context requires review.
notes: Built in 1879 by the Canal Commissioners at state expense. The exact waterway, city-boundary status, dimensions and later history require engineering and map confirmation.

address_historical: Eighteenth Street railroad crossing
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago and affected railroads
structural_system: wrought-iron superstructure; two truss-girder spans
postfire_code_context: Durable iron infrastructure aligned with post-fire material preferences, though grade separation was its primary purpose.
notes: Completed December 18, 1878 and put in operation February 7, 1879. Andreas reports $11,194 cost, two 142-foot truss-girder spans, a 20-foot roadway and six-foot sidewalks. Not counted as 1879 construction.

canonical_name: Chicago fire-alarm system Stock Yards extension
alternate_names: Stock Yards aerial fire-alarm lines and stations
address_historical: Stock Yards district, Town of Lake
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago; Town of Lake stations
structural_system: aerial telegraph wire, alarm stations and Tooker keyless-door box retrofits
postfire_code_context: The extension increased fire-detection coverage and retrofitted 72 existing boxes with keyless doors, a direct post-fire life-safety investment.
notes: Andreas reports extension of aerial lines to the Stock Yards district in the Town of Lake, establishment of fire-alarm stations, and Tooker keyless-door attachments on 72 existing boxes. It is a network event extending beyond the 1879 municipal boundary, not one building.

alternate_names: Bemis & McAvoy brewery ice house phase
address_historical: Bemis & McAvoy brewery complex, east side
structural_system: ice-house construction; material not stated
postfire_code_context: An industrial outbuilding erected after the citywide wood-building restriction; material and permit compliance remain unverified.
notes: Andreas says two east-side ice houses were erected in 1878 and 1879. This row assigns one phase to 1879 but does not infer dimensions, material or a precise address; component identity needs brewery and permit records.

address_historical: Immediately south of the Bemis & McAvoy brewhouse
structural_system: substantial brick masonry
postfire_code_context: Brick office construction complied with the post-1874 restriction on new wood buildings.
notes: Erected in 1879. Andreas describes a substantial two-story brick office south of the brewhouse with the main business office and billiard rooms.

address_historical: Behind Holy Family Church
address_modern: Holy Family Church complex near 1080 W Roosevelt Rd
original_use: Catholic sodality meetings, reading room and libraries
structural_system: material not stated
postfire_code_context: A large institutional addition in the post-fire city; material and exact fireproofing require parish or permit records.
notes: Erected behind the church in 1879 at a reported cost of $40,000. Andreas describes meeting rooms and halls, a reading room, and two libraries totaling approximately 3,000 volumes.

canonical_name: Academy of the Sacred Heart chapel
address_historical: Adjoining the Academy of the Sacred Heart
address_modern: West Side academy complex; exact parcel unresolved
structural_system: material not stated
postfire_code_context: Post-fire institutional construction; exact material and code compliance are not documented in the located narrative.
notes: Andreas reports that a chapel was built adjoining the academy in 1879. No separate street number, architect, dimensions or material were located, so the row remains a named complex phase rather than a guessed standalone footprint.

address_historical: Dashiel Street and Thirty-seventh Street; later Union Avenue and 37th Street
owner_or_developer: Nativity of Our Lord Catholic parish
structural_system: masonry Romanesque-Gothic church; detailed materials not stated
postfire_code_context: Masonry church construction complied with the post-1874 prohibition on new wood buildings.
notes: Foundation work began in 1876, the cornerstone was laid October 28, 1876, and the church was completed and dedicated September 1, 1879. Historical street-name/address reconciliation and the survival of specific 1879 fabric need architectural survey.

canonical_name: St. Stephen German Evangelical Lutheran Church repair and refit
address_historical: Northwest corner Wentworth Avenue and Twenty-fifth Street
address_modern: Approx. W 25th St and S Wentworth Ave
owner_or_developer: St. Stephen German Evangelical Lutheran congregation
structural_system: pre-existing frame church on brick basement; repaired and refitted
postfire_code_context: The retained frame superstructure was pre-existing; the 1879 work was repair and refit rather than prohibited new frame construction.
notes: The congregation organized May 1, purchased the property September 1 for a reported $10,475, thoroughly repaired and refitted the approximately 1,000-seat church, installed an organ reported at $3,000, and dedicated it in fall 1879.

address_historical: Thirty-sixth Street and Vincennes Avenue
structural_system: masonry church; exact system not independently verified
postfire_code_context: A church dated to 1879 would fall under the post-1874 citywide wood-building prohibition, but material and permit confirmation remain required.
notes: WBEZ reports the church was built in 1879; WTTW corroborates the 3600 South Vincennes identity and later Ida B. Wells Homes context. Primary church, permit or contemporary newspaper confirmation is still needed.

alternate_names: Kingsbury Music Hall; New Chicago Theatre; Metropolitan Theatre
address_historical: 66-72 West Randolph Street with former Clark Street entrance
address_modern: Randolph Street theater district near Clark Street
structural_system: pre-existing masonry theater; exterior and interior thoroughly renovated
postfire_code_context: The refit of an existing post-fire assembly building should be evaluated against contemporary theater egress and fire-safety requirements.
notes: A Chicago Tribune account dated August 30, 1879 describes thorough exterior and interior renovation and reopening as the Olympic. This is an adaptive-reuse phase, not a new 1879 building.

canonical_name: Farwell Hall YMCA gymnasium and bath addition
alternate_names: Farwell Hall Young Men's Christian Association facilities
address_historical: Farwell Hall, downtown Chicago; exact 1879 street number unresolved
owner_or_developer: Young Men's Christian Association of Chicago
structural_system: material and structural system not stated
postfire_code_context: A public-health and recreation addition after the fire; material and fire-code details require YMCA property records.
notes: YMCA of Metropolitan Chicago's institutional chronology states that a gymnasium and bath were added to Farwell Hall in 1879. Exact dimensions, architect, materials and address remain unresolved.

canonical_name: C. P. Kimball & Co. carriage building opening
alternate_names: C. P. Kimball carriage manufactory phase
address_historical: Chicago; exact 1879 address unresolved
structural_system: five-floor industrial building; material not stated
postfire_code_context: A multi-story industrial occupancy in the post-fire city; the building's material and permit history are not identified.
notes: Andreas says the company opened its building in 1879 and describes the whole building as 40 by 160 feet with five floors. A larger Wabash-and-Harrison facility described elsewhere may be later, so that address is not assigned here. Not counted as verified new construction.
